newsitem.title: MEXICO: Cemex shares miss out on Mexico party.
newsitem.headline: Cemex shares miss out on Mexico party.

text.p: Cement firm Cemex's B series shares had chalked up a hefty 13.6 percent gain for the year to Monday in dollar terms, but have since lagged the market due to uncertainty among investors, analysts say.
Cemex was one of just three stocks that did not benefit from a euphoric session for the Mexican bourse on Wednesday, following news the country had pre-paid its debt to the U.S. Treasury.
Analysts said Cemex was weighed down by worries that new government regulations could hit its Colombian subsidiary, Cementos Diamante.

The Colombian government announced on Monday it would levy a six percent tariff on the discount between loans raised by Colombian firms on the international markets and comparative rates available locally.

"Cemex plans to complete the expansion of its Cementos Diamante Ibague plant in Colombia, for which the company has said it will contract debt of $250-300 million," said Paul Rodriguez, Latin American cement company analyst at Caspian Securities.
Nonetheless, it remains to be seen whether it is up to Cementos Diamante to contract the debt, or will fall to Cemex in its capacity as holding company.
Cemex's 1997 net earnings would decline by one percent, at the most, if Cementos Diamante were to contract the debt, Rodriguez said.

"It depends on when they contract the debt, which may be half way through the year. But if Cemex contracts it as the holding company, I do not think the tariff would affect them at all, so the stock should not be falling the way it is," he added.

Carmen Slade, of Salomon Brothers, thinks investors may also be concerned over news Portugal's largest cement producer Cimpor-Cimentos de Portugal will be buying the cement business of Brazilian company Serrana.

"I do not think people weighed up these news items carefully, maybe they got nervous and decided to take profits, but I don't think the news affects Cemex's fundamentals," Slade said in a telephone interview.
Slade added some investors may believe Cemex "lost" Serrana, in its bid to enter the Brazilian market.
"Cemex themselves said at the end of November they would not bid for Serrana or Cimento Caue," she said.
